summaries.summary: NLP models capture unwanted biases and stereotypes from training data, raising concerns about socioeconomic, ethnic and gender discrimination in public deployment.
Studies identify algorithmic bias in NLP applications, including Google autocomplete suggestions, advertisement delivery systems, and coreference resolution systems.
Language modelling has downstream applications such as text generation, is vulnerable to gender bias, and this study introduces a loss function equalizing gendered word pair probabilities.

Contributions include loss-function bias alleviation, equalizing male and female word probabilities, end-to-end debiasing, comparison with existing methods, and best results with counterfactual data augmentation.
Bias research in NLP applications has increased, with relevant work divided into word embedding debiasing and data debiasing by preprocessing.
Training data uses Daily Mail news articles with 219,506 articles, randomly subsampled to 5% of text and around 8.25 million tokens.

The LSTM language model uses pre-trained 300-dimensional GloVe, 2 hidden layers with 300 units, sequence length 35, learning rate 20, dropout 0.25, gradient clip 0.25, 150 epochs, batch size 48, and early stopping patience 5.
Language models are usually trained using cross-entropy loss, with cross-entropy loss at time step INLINEFORM0 given as INLINEFORM1.
INLINEFORM0 is the vocabulary, INLINEFORM1 is the one hot vector of ground truth, and INLINEFORM2 indicates the output softmax probability.
A loss term INLINEFORM0 is introduced to equalize predicted probabilities of gender pairs such as woman and man, expressed as INLINEFORM1.
INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 are corresponding gender pairs, INLINEFORM2 is their set size, INLINEFORM3 is output softmax probability, and gender pairs from BIBREF7 neutralize only gender information.
INLINEFORM0 is a hyperparameter, INLINEFORM1 is corpus size, and INLINEFORM2 encourages convergence toward a minimum with the lowest gender bias.
Language models are evaluated using perplexity and an array of bias metrics, with gender pairs from BIBREF7 containing 223 pairs and all other words considered gender-neutral.
Co-occurrence bias compares occurrences of gender-neutral words with female and male words in model-generated texts, defining gender bias as INLINEFORM0.

INLINEFORM0 is a set of gender-neutral words, INLINEFORM1 is occurrences with gender INLINEFORM3, co-occurrences use a sliding window of size 10, and words occurring more than 20 times are considered.
A normalized version of INLINEFORM0 is evaluated as conditional co-occurrence bias, INLINEFORM1, defined as INLINEFORM2.
The paragraph states where INLINEFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is less affected by disparity in male and female word distribution, and the ratio of occurrence of male and female words, INLINEFORM1, is reported as INLINEFORM2.
Causal testing exposes models to paired samples differing only in one attribute, with output disparity interpreted as bias related to that attribute.

Causal occupation bias evaluation is limited to gender-neutral occupations using two template sets, with the first measuring occupation word probabilities conditioned on gender information in the seed.
The vertical bar separates the seed sequence from the target occupation, and causal occupation bias conditioned on gender is measured as INLINEFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a set of gender-neutral occupations, INLINEFORM1 is the gender pairs set size, and the second template set captures gendered word probabilities conditioned on occupation words.
Causal occupation bias conditioned on occupation is represented as INLINEFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a set of gender-neutral occupations, INLINEFORM1 is the gender pairs set size, and INLINEFORM2 is the softmax probability of man for the seed sequence The doctor is a.
Both INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 contribute to gender bias in model-generated texts, while INLINEFORM2 is more easily influenced by general disparity in male and female word probabilities.

Gender-neutral occupations measure embedding bias, defined as the difference between Euclidean distances of occupation words to male words and female counterparts, with INLINEFORM1 defined as INLINEFORM2.
INLINEFORM0 is a set of gender-neutral occupations, INLINEFORM1 is the gender pairs set size, and INLINEFORM2 is the word-to-vector dictionary.
CDA swaps all gendered words using a bidirectional dictionary of gender pairs, creating a dataset twice the original size with identical contextual distributions for both genders.
The bias regularization method of BIBREF5 debiases word embeddings during language model training, uses hyperparameter tuning for the best regularization coefficient, and is later called REG.

Experiments measure training data co-occurrence bias, tune INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1, test CDA, REG, and their combination, and evaluate bias using template datasets and 10,000 documents of 500 words each.

Table TABREF12 shows the baseline amplifies training data bias, while the method at INLINEFORM2 value of 1 reduces INLINEFORM3 by 58.95%, INLINEFORM4 by 45.74%, INLINEFORM5 by 100%, INLINEFORM6 by 98.52%, and INLINEFORM7 by 98.98%.
REG is not very effective in mitigating bias, achieves the best perplexity, has a slight regularization effect, and is outperformed by the loss function in INLINEFORM0.
The method outperforms CDA in INLINEFORM0, INLINEFORM1, and INLINEFORM2, while CDA achieves slightly better co-occurrence biases INLINEFORM3 and INLINEFORM4 and better perplexity.
The combination of CDA and the loss function outperforms all methods in all measures of biases without compromising perplexity.
The research proposes a new approach for mitigating gender bias in neural language models and emphasizes loss function based debiasing as effective, powerful, and generalizable.
All experimented debiasing techniques rely on a predefined set of gender pairs, which is a limitation and leaves gender associated words without pairs, like pregnant, improperly treated.
Future work includes a context-aware loss function distinguishing unbiased and biased gendered word mentions and exploring application of the method to mitigating racial bias.
The authors thank Sam Bowman, Shikha Bordia, Cuiying Yang, Gang Qian, Xiyu Miao, Qianyi Fan, Tian Liu, Stanislav Sobolevsky, and reviewers.
